card.hook: Everyone squeezes under the big neon arch, and fair enough, it's a show. But a few steps down the strip there's a little lane strung with bare bulbs, and most people march right past it.
card.stand_here: Stand on Soi 13/4, a narrow side lane about a third of the way down Walking Street from the arch (the main strip lies to the south-west). Face along the lane so the string lights glow above and behind your subject, and check the exact spot on the day.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the lane and the lights overhead. Switch to 2x for portraits, because it flatters faces and keeps the background softer. Try 0.5x only if you want the whole line of bulbs stretching above you.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put your subject on one of the vertical lines, then tap their face and slide the brightness a little darker so the bulbs stay warm instead of blowing out.
card.best_time: Go after dark, when the string lights are on and the street is open to walkers. Earlier in the evening the lane is likely to be quieter.
card.selfie_here: Try the Soi 13/4 string-light lane: warm light and fewer people make it a better backdrop than the busy main strip. Use the front camera and hold it a bit high. For the classic arrival selfie, switch to 0.5x under the illuminated arch at the Beach Road end and get the neon over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the slight rise on the Beach Road side of the northern arch and shoot south (around 21:00 works), while you stand under the illuminated arch with the crowd moving around you.
card.rules_and_safety: Selfie sticks are listed as allowed. Keep your phone out of the venues, don't photograph bar staff, and expect street performers and animals to want a tip if you photograph them. It's crowded and pickpockets operate, so carry only the essentials.
card.challenge: Get one shot where the bulbs look like a glowing roof over your friend's head, with nobody else in the frame. Bonus points if they pretend not to notice.
card.good_to_know: Walking Street began as a road serving a fishing village. In the 1960s and 70s it changed to cater for visiting American soldiers on leave. It was closed to traffic in the evenings after a run of car accidents in the 1990s, and a large video sign went up at the Beach Road entrance in March 2010.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on Soi 13/4, a narrow side lane about a third of the way down Walking Street from the arch (the main strip lies to the south-west). Face along the lane so the string lights glow above and behind your subject, and check the exact spot on the day.

card.hook: You'll be handed a hard hat at the door, and that's your first clue this place is different. It's a giant wooden temple that's been under construction since 1981, and it looks even better with the sea behind it.
card.stand_here: Head to the sea-facing waterfront platform at the water's edge, where the phone icon on the map marks the spot. It's inside the ticketed grounds, so go in first, then turn around and face back up at the building.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole structure and the sea in one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer, more natural view, then use 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out carved figures and spire details.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the building, then slide the brightness a little darker so the bright sky doesn't wash out that lovely carved wood.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is the time guides recommend for the view from the sea side. Go earlier in the day if you'd like fewer people in your shot.
card.selfie_here: Try the sea-facing platform at the water's edge, where the sanctuary's full height rises behind you. Use the front camera, hold it a bit low and let the building tower over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to shoot from the hilltop viewpoint just past the entrance, while you stand in front of the façade so the sea fills the rest of the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Hard hats are required inside. Drones and professional setups usually need permission first, so check the official site for hours and ticket rules. Take care when shooting near steps or elevated areas.
card.challenge: Find the carved face you like best, then get a close-up of it and a selfie of you pulling the same expression.
card.good_to_know: The Sanctuary of Truth is carved almost entirely from wood, and it's still unfinished. Work began in 1981 and carries on today. The grounds cover 13 hectares, and the tallest spire reaches 105 metres. The design draws on the temples of Ayutthaya and on Hindu and Buddhist ideas.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head to the sea-facing waterfront platform at the water's edge, where the phone icon on the map marks the spot. It's inside the ticketed grounds, so go in first, then turn around and face back up at the building.

card.hook: Plain beach photos all look alike, but nobody will wonder where you were when there are giant letters spelling out the city in front of the bay. This spot is about the sign, with Pattaya's long curve of sand and sea behind it.
card.stand_here: Head for the Pattaya City Sign on the hillside, towards the north end of Beach Road. Face the lettering with the beach and sea spread out behind it, so the big letters sit in the foreground.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x so the sign and the bay both fit. If you're close to the lettering, switch to zoom 0.5x to keep every letter in. Try zoom 2x-5x (depending on your phone) to pick out boats on the water or Koh Larn offshore.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines and place the lettering along the lower third, with the sea and sky filling the rest.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is lovely, because the sun sets over the water to the west. If you visit the hilltop viewpoint on Khao Phra Tamnak, go early, as tour groups crowd it.
card.selfie_here: Try the palm-lined walkway along Pattaya Beach Promenade, early in the morning when it's quieter, with the sea behind you. Use the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to fit in more of the scene, and keep the palms and sea over your shoulder.
card.rules_and_safety: The sign isn't listed as a paid spot, but access and any opening times can change, so check the official site or local signage before you go.
card.challenge: Take one frame with people in it and one without, then pick which one tells the better story.
card.good_to_know: Pattaya Beach is the long curve of sand and sea that gives the city its postcard look. Photo guides describe the sign as a popular photo spot with a view over both the city and the sea. For a wide panorama of the whole bay, the hilltop viewpoint on Khao Phra Tamnak shows the hotel strip following the shoreline and Koh Larn offshore.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the Pattaya City Sign on the hillside, towards the north end of Beach Road. Face the lettering with the beach and sea spread out behind it, so the big letters sit in the foreground.

card.hook: Jomtien Beach never holds still. There's a parasail drifting past, a jet ski buzzing by and a windsurfer leaning into the wind, so your photo almost always has something going on in it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the sand near the promenade on Jomtien Beach, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Face the gulf, which is west, and keep the horizon level using your gridlines.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for the main sunset shot. Go to 0.5x for the big sweep of the bay and the promenade. Try 2x or 5x (higher zooms depend on your phone) to pick out a kitesurfer or a single boat.
card.make_it_pop: Tap the brightest part of the sky, then drag the slider down a little so it gets darker and the sunset colours stay rich.
card.best_time: Go late in the afternoon, up to sunset, because the beach faces west and the sky colours over the water. About 5:30-6:30 PM is typical, but it shifts with the season, so check the sunset time for your date.
card.selfie_here: Find the colourful seahorse sculpture on the sand and stand beside it with the sea and beach behind you. Use the front camera, and try 0.5x if your phone has it to fit more in. One guide suggests sunrise there for the backdrop.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand on the beach a few steps back from the decorated 'Jomthien Pattaya' arch sign, while you stand by the arch, so the whole arch fits in the frame with you.
card.rules_and_safety: Camping and starting bonfires on the beach without authorization is prohibited. Smoking on the beach is also against Thai law and can bring heavy fines. Anglers are reminded not to cast lines near swimming areas, so keep an eye out if you're in the water.
card.challenge: Add a foreground, like footprints, a beach chair or someone walking by, then wait for a kitesurfer to cross the brightest part of the sky and tap before they leave the frame.
card.good_to_know: Jomtien is about 3 km south of Pattaya and roughly 165 km south-east of Bangkok. The beach is lined with high-rise condos, hotels and restaurants, and it's popular for swimming and windsurfing. If you have time, Jomtien Heads Viewpoint gives a wide view south over the curve of the coast, with Koh Larn beyond.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the sand near the promenade on Jomtien Beach, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Face the gulf, which is west, and keep the horizon level using your gridlines.

card.hook: The best seat at Pattaya Floating Market is a boat seat, down at water level, with vendor boats drifting past and stilt shops lining the banks. It's the classic view, and it feels like you've landed inside a postcard.
card.stand_here: Head for the phone icon on the map, right at Pattaya Floating Market on Sukhumvit Road (451/304 Moo 12). For the classic shot, sit low in a boat on the main canal and face along the water, with a paddle boat in front of you.
card.zoom: Use zoom 1x from the boat for vendor boats and stilt shops. Switch to 0.5x on the walkways to fit in the canal and bridge railings, and use 2x for stall details.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, tap a boat, then slide the brightness down a touch so the sky and water don't wash out.
card.best_time: Aim for late afternoon, when the light is softer and the water glares less. Wait for a calm patch of water and the reflections will look much cleaner.
card.selfie_here: Try a flower- or lantern-decorated bridge over the canals, ideally after your longboat ride, or look for the market's 'hanging bridge' walkway over the water. Use the front camera at 0.5x and keep the bridge and canal over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand back from one of the wooden bridges where the canal paths meet, while you stand on the bridge with the canal and wooden buildings behind you, so bridges, boats and shopfronts all fit in.
card.rules_and_safety: Entry is ticketed and boat rides cost extra, so check the entry fee and opening hours when you arrive. Ask first before taking a close photo of a vendor or their stall. Selfie sticks are listed as allowed, but that listing may be out of date. Hold your phone with both hands on the boat.
card.challenge: Get a paddle boat in the foreground with the stilt shops running off behind it, and see if you can catch a boat gliding through the frame.
card.good_to_know: Pattaya Floating Market is a canal-side market built on the water, with wooden stilt shops and vendor boats along the banks. Timber walkways, bridge railings and colourful stalls are all close together, so there's plenty to shoot. The boat ride is the main way to get that water-level angle.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Head for the phone icon on the map, right at Pattaya Floating Market on Sukhumvit Road (451/304 Moo 12). For the classic shot, sit low in a boat on the main canal and face along the water, with a paddle boat in front of you.

card.hook: Some photo stops are about the view. This one is about the fun of being in the picture, so don't stress about a perfect shot. Just get a good one of you and your crew.
card.stand_here: Art in Paradise Pattaya is number 6 on the map, and the phone icon sits right at the attraction itself, so there's no extra walk once you arrive. Stand a few steps back, face your subject squarely and hold your phone at chest or face height.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for most shots, because it keeps things looking natural. Switch to 0.5x in tight spaces or when the subject is big, and keep people away from the edges so faces don't stretch. Zoom 2x is good for close-up portraits of friends.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines to keep straight edges level, then tap your friend's face and drag the slider to darker if bright parts look washed out.
card.best_time: Check the official site for visiting information before you go. Arriving earlier in the day or on a weekday may mean fewer people in your shots.
card.selfie_here: Use the front camera, switch to 0.5x to squeeze more in, and hold your phone a little above eye level so the background fits over your shoulder. If you want a photo of the whole group, bring a friend or ask another visitor or a member of staff to take it.
card.rules_and_safety: Rules on photography and entry can change, so check the official site before you go.
card.challenge: Take one wide shot of the whole scene and one closer shot with the same pose, then see which one your friends like best.
card.good_to_know: Art in Paradise Pattaya is a visitor attraction in Pattaya, and it's number 6 on our map. Inside, floor markers show where to hold your camera for each scene. Take a few frames from slightly different angles, because small changes in position can make a big difference.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Art in Paradise Pattaya is number 6 on the map, and the phone icon sits right at the attraction itself, so there's no extra walk once you arrive. Stand a few steps back, face your subject squarely and hold your phone at chest or face height.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names an outdoor spot where the museum is behind the visitor, so I am not giving a selfie spot or a passer-by spot. The pages describe the inside of the museum, not its exterior. Named indoor zones include the Elephant 3D painting area, the Underwater World scene, the Classic Art Zone and the Dinosaur Zone (Trip.com 2026 guide; Wonderful Museums guide). Floor markers show the camera position for each scene (Wonderful Museums; The Thai Tourism guide), but these are interior exhibits, not outdoor spots with the building behind. Pages say to bring a friend, or ask staff or another visitor, to take your photo (Your Thai Guide; Gap Photography). No page states a selfie stick or tripod rule. The venue is on Pattaya 2nd Road / Pattaya Sai 2 Road (Moo 9), but no page describes the street-side frontage. I did not check the supplied coordinates against a map.

card.hook: Picture a 111-metre curve of wood and glass, palm trees out front, and a hotel tower poking up through the roof. That's Central Pattaya, and it's hard to miss on this bay.
card.stand_here: Stand near ซอยพัทยา 9 (Pattaya Beach Soi 9), at the phone icon on the map, about 120 m north-west of the numbered pin. Face south-east and the mall's beach side is right in front of you.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the whole curved front and the palms in one frame. Switch to 1x for a calmer view of the entrance and plaza. Then try 2x-5x (depending on your phone) for the Hilton tower and the details on the front.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines so the building's edges stay straight, and if the glass looks too dark, tap the brightest part of the sky.
card.best_time: Late afternoon is worth a try for softer light on the front. After dark the lit-up building should look good in night mode, so rest your elbows against your body to keep the phone steady.
card.selfie_here: Head to the 2nd-floor beachfront exit near the Supersports store, where the Central and Hilton logos sit on a modern building. Use the front camera at 0.5x and let the mall show behind your shoulder. For a sunset selfie, the sea-facing promenade across from the mall also puts the building behind you.
card.ask_someone: Ask a friendly passer-by on the beach in front of the mall to take your photo, and stand so the mall, the sea and the sand are all in the frame behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: The mall is a public shopping centre, so check the official site for opening times and any rules about photography inside.
card.challenge: Take two shots: one wide with a palm tree framing the side, then one upright with the Hilton tower rising above the roofline. Bonus points if the verticals are dead straight.
card.good_to_know: Central Pattaya opened in 2009 and is described as the largest beachfront shopping centre in Southeast Asia. It has seven floors and more than 370 shops, plus a cinema, a bowling alley and food courts. The Hilton Pattaya sits on top of the mall, which is why you can spot it from far along the bay.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand near ซอยพัทยา 9 (Pattaya Beach Soi 9), at the phone icon on the map, about 120 m north-west of the numbered pin. Face south-east and the mall's beach side is right in front of you.

card.hook: Picture a ferry nosing in, a few boats bobbing at anchor, and the whole curve of Pattaya Beach sweeping away behind them. That's the view from the end of Bali Hai Pier, and it takes no planning at all.
card.stand_here: Walk to the outer end of Bali Hai Pier, right where the phone icon sits on the map. Face back across the bay, so the boats are close to you and the beach curves away to the north behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to get the whole bay, boats and beach curve in one frame. Switch to 1x for a more natural look, then try 2x or 5x (depending on your phone) to pick out a single ferry or the far end of the beach.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on the gridlines, put the horizon on a line so it stays level, and keep a boat or two in the lower part of the frame leading the eye to the beach.
card.best_time: Late afternoon, roughly 5:00 to 6:30 PM, gives you golden light. Early morning is lovely too, with softer light.
card.selfie_here: Head for the far end of the pier walkway, beside the 'Pattaya City' letters. Bloggers single this corner out as the photo spot. Use the front camera at 0.5x and hold your phone a bit low so the bay fits over your shoulder.
card.ask_someone: Ask a passer-by to stand at the outer end of the pier deck while you stand in front of them on the deck, so the bay and the pier both fit in the frame.
card.rules_and_safety: Photos from ground level are fine, but be respectful of crew and passengers, and stay clear of the gangways when ferries are docking. Drones need permits under Thai aviation rules. One reviewer says the pier isn't really safe at night, so this is one for daylight.
card.challenge: Catch a ferry, an anchored boat and the whole beach curve in one level-horizon shot, and no one gets to say you only photographed the water.
card.good_to_know: Bali Hai Pier is a working pier on the Pattaya waterfront, with ferries and anchored boats in front of the open bay. Fancy a different angle? Khao Phra Tamnak gives a high view down onto the pier, bay and city, and Laem Bali Hai shows the lighthouse with the pier and boats beyond it. Which one suits you depends on how much walking you want to do.

card.hook: You're about to tower over Wat Arun and nobody will mind. Everything here is built at 1:25, so the temples fit neatly on your screen.
card.stand_here: Stand at the entrance of the Thai section of Mini Siam, where the temple models begin. The phone icon on the map is right there, so there's no extra walk. Face the models of the Emerald Buddha temple and Wat Arun, with the park's gardens behind them.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 0.5x to fit the temples and the gardens in one shot. Switch to 1x for a single temple, then try 2x to 5x for roofs and spires (higher zooms depend on your phone).
card.make_it_pop: Hold your phone at eye level, keep the temples in the middle with garden around them, and try portrait mode on a single model for a softer background.
card.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon is best. The light is softer and there are fewer people wandering into your shot.
card.selfie_here: Take it at the entrance of the Thai zone with the temple models behind you. Use the front camera, try 0.5x if your phone has it, and keep the temples over your shoulder. If you have time, the path beside the water between the zones works too, with the Sydney Opera House replica behind you.
card.rules_and_safety: Keep to the paths and don't step into the replica areas. Drones aren't permitted. Ask before including other visitors in your photos. The sun can be brutal, so bring water and sunscreen. It's a ticketed park, so check the official site for entry details and opening times before you go.
card.challenge: Take a shot with the garden behind the temples that makes a friend ask, 'Wait, is that real?'
card.good_to_know: Mini Siam's founder, Kasem Kasemkietsakul, wanted famous landmarks together in one place so visitors could learn about architecture. The first model built was the Democracy Monument from Bangkok. A small stretch of water divides the Thai section from the Mini Europe section, where the Sydney Opera House replica sits against it.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand at the entrance of the Thai section of Mini Siam, where the temple models begin. The phone icon on the map is right there, so there's no extra walk. Face the models of the Emerald Buddha temple and Wat Arun, with the park's gardens behind them.

card.hook: Most of Pattaya's beaches come with a busy road right beside them, but Wong Amat doesn't. Here you get low rocks, fishing boats and a big open horizon over the bay.
card.stand_here: Walk down Soi Naklua 18 to the sand, then turn toward the left-hand rocky end of the beach. Stand among the low rocks and face the sea, so the horizon fills your screen.
card.zoom: Start at 1x for sunset and silhouette shots of the rocks and horizon. Try 0.5x to catch more of the curving shoreline, or 2x or more (depending on your phone) to pick out a single fishing boat.
card.make_it_pop: Turn on gridlines, put the horizon on the upper or lower line and keep it level, then tap the bright part of the sky and drag the brightness down until the rocks go dark and the colours get rich.
card.best_time: Sunset is the favourite, roughly 17:30 to 18:30 according to one guide. Another guide suggests mornings if you want quieter light.
card.selfie_here: Use the rocky stretch at the left-hand end of the beach, reached from Soi Naklua 18, which guides call a strong angle for sea-and-sky shots. Use the front camera, try 0.5x, and keep the sea and sunset sky over your shoulder. The rocks at the north end of the beach are another good spot, and reviewers say it has the prettiest views.
card.ask_someone: Stand on the sand in front of the Pullman hotel's beach club with the beach and sea behind you, and ask a passer-by to shoot from the beach side facing you (check it works for you when you get there).
card.rules_and_safety: Parking is very limited near the beach end, and some shore areas may mean passing through resort grounds, so stay on public paths. If you swim near the rocks, wear water shoes to protect your feet.
card.challenge: Put one dark rock in the bottom corner, the horizon on a gridline, and a fishing boat sitting on the water. That's your whole shot.
card.good_to_know: Wong Amat is about 1.3 km long, on the Nakluea Bay peninsula in northern Pattaya. The first hotel here opened in 1960, and the beach is named after its original owner, Boonwong Amatayakul. The condo towers behind the sand went up in the 2010s.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Walk down Soi Naklua 18 to the sand, then turn toward the left-hand rocky end of the beach. Stand among the low rocks and face the sea, so the horizon fills your screen.

card.hook: Here's the honest bit: from this hill, Pattaya Park Tower is a small tower in a big, busy scene. That's the charm, because you get to see the whole district stretched out beneath it.
card.stand_here: Stand on the observation platform next to the Big Buddha Temple on Phratamnak Hill, in the south of Pattaya. Face south-west and look out over Jomtien, and the tower is off in the distance.
card.zoom: Start at zoom 1x for one wide shot of the whole view. Then try zoom 2x to 5x (depending on your phone) to bring the tower closer. Zoom 0.5x makes the tower tiny, so save it for when you've got something fun in the foreground.
card.make_it_pop: Switch on the gridlines, put the tower on one of the vertical lines, tap the tower, then drag the brightness slider a touch darker so the sky keeps its colour.
card.best_time: Pick a clear day, because haze can wash out a faraway tower. Morning or later in the day is usually kinder to the colours than midday, when the light is softer and the air is cooler.
card.selfie_here: Turn on the front camera, try zoom 0.5x to squeeze in more scenery, and stand with the view over your shoulder. The tower will be small behind you, so take a few shots and pick your favourite.
card.rules_and_safety: The platform is free to use, but it sits beside a place of worship, so dress respectfully. If you rest your elbows on the rail to steady your phone, only do it where it's safe.
card.challenge: Take two photos from the same spot: one wide shot of the whole district, and one zoomed shot where the tower is the star. Which one would you frame?
card.good_to_know: Pattaya Park Tower is a tall landmark on the Jomtien side of Pattaya. It has a viewing deck, but that's inside the building, so it's no good for photographing the tower itself. For a different angle, Thappraya Road has a wide panorama of the northern Jomtien shoreline, taken from the beach near the corner, with the tower in the frame.
card.stand_here_before_gps_rule: Stand on the observation platform next to the Big Buddha Temple on Phratamnak Hill, in the south of Pattaya. Face south-west and look out over Jomtien, and the tower is off in the distance.

selfie_research.notes: No page I found names a spot outside the tower where a visitor has Pattaya Park Tower behind them, so I have not listed a selfie spot. The tower is on Thappraya Road in Jomtien Beach (https://www.travalot.com/top-places/pattaya-park-tower) and stands within Pattaya Park Beach Resort (https://forevervacation.com/pattaya/the-pattaya-park-tower). The photo spots the pages do name are inside the tower and face outward toward the view, so the tower is not the backdrop: the 55th-floor observation deck (https://www.travalot.com/top-places/pattaya-park-tower), a small outdoor area on an upper floor where you shoot through a safety grille, and a 56th-floor area with a grate (https://www.trip.com/moments/poi-pattaya-park-tower-95140/). The Bali Hai Pier and Pattaya City sign results are a different landmark, so I excluded them. No page gives selfie stick or tripod rules, so I left rules empty. No page gives a safety point for this tower beyond the grille note, which I left out of the safety field.
